Permutation and bootstrap tests

Source: vignettes/resampling.Rmd
resampling.Rmd

F and t tests rest on the model’s distributional assumptions and, for mixed models, on approximate degrees of freedom. With few experimental units, skewed residuals or a GLMM, resampling tests are a useful check. predictmeans has:

  • permmodels(): permutation tests of the terms and coefficients of lm, glm, aov, gls, lme and lmer models;
  • permlmer() and permanova.lmer(): permutation likelihood-ratio tests for lmer models, including tests of random effects;
  • bootmodels(): parametric bootstrap tests for lmer and glmer models.

The results of permmodels() and bootmodels() can be passed to predictmeans() and contrastmeans() (argument permlist), which then give resampling p-values for pairwise comparisons and contrasts.

The examples below use 99 or 199 resamples so that they run quickly; use 999 or more in practice. The smallest p-value possible is 1/(number of resamples + 1). ncore sets the number of cores used for the refits (ncore = 1 here, as for CRAN checks); seed makes the results reproducible.

library(predictmeans)
Oats <- as.data.frame(nlme::Oats)
Oats$nitro <- factor(Oats$nitro)
fm <- lmer(yield ~ nitro * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Oats)

Permutation tests of terms and coefficients

For linear models the response is permuted. For mixed models the residuals are first decorrelated with the Cholesky factor of their estimated covariance, permuted, and correlated again (Lee and Braun 2012), so each permuted data set keeps the model’s correlation structure; the model is then refitted to each.

perm <- permmodels(fm, nperm = 199, ncore = 1, seed = 1)
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>                            Estimate Std. Error      df t value Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)                 80.0000     9.1070 16.0816  8.7844   0.0000
#> nitro0.2                    18.5000     7.6829 45.0000  2.4079   0.0202
#> nitro0.4                    34.6667     7.6829 45.0000  4.5122   0.0000
#> nitro0.6                    44.8333     7.6829 45.0000  5.8354   0.0000
#> VarietyMarvellous            6.6667     9.7150 30.2308  0.6862   0.4978
#> VarietyVictory              -8.5000     9.7150 30.2308 -0.8749   0.3885
#> nitro0.2:VarietyMarvellous   3.3333    10.8653 45.0000  0.3068   0.7604
#> nitro0.4:VarietyMarvellous  -4.1667    10.8653 45.0000 -0.3835   0.7032
#> nitro0.6:VarietyMarvellous  -4.6667    10.8653 45.0000 -0.4295   0.6696
#> nitro0.2:VarietyVictory     -0.3333    10.8653 45.0000 -0.0307   0.9757
#> nitro0.4:VarietyVictory      4.6667    10.8653 45.0000  0.4295   0.6696
#> nitro0.6:VarietyVictory      2.1667    10.8653 45.0000  0.1994   0.8428
#>                            Perm_p_value
#> (Intercept)                          NA
#> nitro0.2                          0.020
#> nitro0.4                          0.005
#> nitro0.6                          0.005
#> VarietyMarvellous                 0.495
#> VarietyVictory                    0.350
#> nitro0.2:VarietyMarvellous        0.775
#> nitro0.4:VarietyMarvellous        0.640
#> nitro0.6:VarietyMarvellous        0.680
#> nitro0.2:VarietyVictory           0.965
#> nitro0.4:VarietyVictory           0.660
#> nitro0.6:VarietyVictory           0.885
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of t test is obtained using '199' permutations.
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#>                   Sum Sq   Mean Sq NumDF DenDF F value Pr(>F) Perm_p_value
#> nitro         20020.5001 6673.5000     3    45 37.6857 0.0000        0.005
#> Variety         526.0575  263.0288     2    10  1.4853 0.2724        0.200
#> nitro:Variety   321.7500   53.6250     6    45  0.3028 0.9322        0.930
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of F test is obtained using '199' permutations.

The tables repeat the model’s tests with a Perm_p_value column: the proportion of permuted statistics at least as large as the observed one.

For lm and aov models, method = "freedman-lane" tests each term by permuting the residuals of the model without that term and adding them back to its fitted values (Freedman and Lane 1983). Permuting the response rejects true null hypotheses too often when a covariate with extreme values is related to the tested term (Anderson and Legendre 1999); Freedman–Lane keeps the level there. It gives the tables only (no refits for permlist), and it is fast:

fm_cars <- lm(mpg ~ wt + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
permmodels(fm_cars, nperm = 999, type = "II", seed = 1, method = "freedman-lane")
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) Perm_p_value
#> (Intercept)   33.9908     1.8878 18.0056   0.0000           NA
#> wt            -3.2056     0.7539 -4.2521   0.0002        0.001
#> factor(cyl)6  -4.2556     1.3861 -3.0702   0.0047        0.009
#> factor(cyl)8  -6.0709     1.6523 -3.6742   0.0010        0.003
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of t test is obtained using '999' Freedman-Lane permutations.
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#> Anova Table (Type II tests)
#> 
#>  Response: mpg
#>               Sum Sq Df F value Pr(>F) Perm_p_value
#> wt          118.2039  1 18.0801 0.0002        0.001
#> factor(cyl)  95.2633  2  7.2856 0.0028        0.005
#> Residuals   183.0586 28                            
#> 
#> Note: Perm_p_value of F test is obtained using '999' Freedman-Lane permutations.

Pairwise comparisons and contrasts

The same refits give permutation p-values for pairwise comparisons, in the pairs table and the legacy p-value matrix:

pm <- predictmeans(fm, "nitro", permlist = perm, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE, ncore = 1)
pm$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "statistic", "p.value", "p.method")]
#>   level1 level2   estimate statistic p.value    p.method
#> 1      0    0.2 -19.500000 -4.396098   0.005 permutation
#> 2      0    0.4 -34.833333 -7.852859   0.005 permutation
#> 3    0.2    0.4 -15.333333 -3.456761   0.005 permutation
#> 4      0    0.6 -44.000000 -9.919400   0.005 permutation
#> 5    0.2    0.6 -24.500000 -5.523302   0.005 permutation
#> 6    0.4    0.6  -9.166667 -2.066542   0.050 permutation

and for contrasts:

cm <- contrast_family(Kmatrix(fm, "nitro"), "trt.vs.ctrl")
contrastmeans(fm, "nitro", ctrmatrix = cm, permlist = perm)[[1]]
#>         Estimate Std. Error t value Permuted Pr(>|t|)
#> 0.2 - 0  19.5000     4.4358  4.3961             0.005
#> 0.4 - 0  34.8333     4.4358  7.8529             0.005
#> 0.6 - 0  44.0000     4.4358  9.9194             0.005
#> attr(,"Note")
#> [1] "The permuted p-value is obtained using '199' permutations."

adj adjusts the permutation p-values with any p.adjust() method or "sidak". "tukey", "scheffe" and "mvt" need the t distribution and are not available with permlist.

Testing random effects: permlmer()

permlmer() compares two nested lmer models with a permutation likelihood-ratio test (Lee and Braun 2012). This is useful for random effects, where the usual chi-square reference distribution is wrong because the null value of a variance lies on the boundary. Does the slope for Days vary between subjects?

fm1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
fm0 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
permlmer(fm0, fm1, nperm = 99, ncore = 1, seed = 1)
#> Data: sleepstudy
#> Models:
#> lmer0: Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject)
#> lmer1: Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject)
#>       npar    AIC    BIC  logLik -2*log(L)  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) Perm-p
#> lmer0    4 1794.5 1807.2 -893.23    1786.5                            
#> lmer1    6 1755.6 1774.8 -871.81    1743.6 42.837  2   4.99e-10   0.01

permanova.lmer() applies the same test to each fixed term of an lmer model in turn (Type I, II or III), for an ANOVA table with permutation p-values.

Parametric bootstrap: bootmodels()

bootmodels() simulates new responses from the model fitted without its fixed effects (an intercept and the same random effects: the global null hypothesis), refits the full model to each and compares the statistics. Unlike permutation, it works for GLMMs. For the clinical trial data (a binomial GLMM):

data(Clinical)
fm_clin <- glmer(cbind(Favorable, Total - Favorable) ~ Treatment + (1 | Clinic),
                 family = binomial, data = Clinical)
boot <- bootmodels(fm_clin, nsim = 99, seed = 1)
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) Boot_p_value
#> (Intercept)    -1.1965     0.5529 -2.1641   0.0305           NA
#> Treatmentdrug   0.7382     0.3004  2.4575   0.0140         0.03
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#>           npar Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Boot_p_value
#> Treatment    1 6.2054  6.2054  6.2054         0.03
#> 
#> Note: Boot_p_value is from '99' parametric bootstrap samples under the global null model.

Its result is used as a permlist; the pairs table then says "bootstrap":

pmb <- predictmeans(fm_clin, "Treatment", permlist = boot, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE,
                    ncore = 1)
pmb$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "p.value", "p.method")]
#>    level1 level2   estimate p.value  p.method
#> 1 control   drug -0.7382041    0.03 bootstrap

Which to use

  • Terms and pairwise comparisons in lm, lme and lmer models: permmodels().
  • Terms of lm and aov models with covariates, especially skewed ones or ones with extreme values: permmodels(method = "freedman-lane").
  • Mixed models with a covariate with extreme values: the Kenward–Roger or Satterthwaite F test (pm_joint(), or anova() of an lmerTest fit); permutation rejected slightly too often there in a simulation study.
  • A variance component, or any comparison of two nested lmer models: permlmer().
  • GLMMs: bootmodels().
  • With large samples and well-behaved residuals the F and t tests (with Kenward–Roger df for lmer) agree closely with these, at a fraction of the time.

References

Anderson, M. J. and Legendre, P. (1999). An empirical comparison of permutation methods for tests of partial regression coefficients in a linear model. Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation 62, 271–303.

Freedman, D. and Lane, D. (1983). A nonstochastic interpretation of reported significance levels. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 1, 292–298.

Lee, O. E. and Braun, T. M. (2012). Permutation tests for random effects in linear mixed models. Biometrics 68, 486–493.
